kurals.tamil:
கருவியும் காலமும் செய்கையும் செய்யும்
அருவினையும் மாண்டது அமைச்சு.
kurals.transliteration:
Karuviyum kaalamum seykaiyum seyyum
Aruvinaiyum maandadhu amaichchu.
kurals.meaning: A true minister is one who excels at thinking through the means needed, the right time, the method of doing it, and the difficult task itself.
kurals.elementary: Think of a team captain planning a school play. A good captain asks: what props do we need, when should we rehearse, how should we do each scene, and what is the hardest part? This kural says a good adviser always thinks about all four of those things.
kurals.university: The couplet opens the Amaichiyal (the section on ministers, chapters 64-73) by defining the minister (amaichu, an abstract noun used for the office-holder) through four objects of deliberation: karuvi (instruments or means, which commentators gloss as troops and wealth), kaalam (the fitting time), seykai (the mode or method of execution) and seyyum aruvinai (the difficult undertaking to be carried out). The verb maandadhu (‘excels, is perfected in’) makes the definition a standard of excellence, not merely a job description. Parimelazhagar and later commentators such as Mu. Varadarasanar read the list as the components of good counsel, which lines up closely with Kautilya’s five limbs of mantra (Arthashastra 1.15). The text is stable across ytamizh.com, thirukkural.net and the older-orthography thirukkural-thamizh.org edition, where it appears as ‘karuviyum kaalamum seykaiyum seyyu / maruvinaiyu maanda thamaichchu’. The difference is only in how the words are split; the reading is the same.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Means to carry out works, command of plenty of men and wealth, allotment of time and place, remedies against dangers, and final success are the five constituents of every council deliberation.”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya lists what every royal council must weigh: the means, the resources, the right time and place, what could go wrong, and how to finish.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar’s four items (means, time, method, the hard task) are almost the same checklist.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close structural parallel from the classical Indian statecraft tradition; Kautilya adds contingency planning and completion.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Or what king, going to make war against another king, sitteth not down first, and consulteth whether he be able with ten thousand to meet him that cometh against him with twenty thousand?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus points out that a sensible king sits down and weighs his resources before starting a war.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural asks the minister to weigh means and difficulty in the same way before acting.
christianity._accuracy_note: Jesus uses this as a parable about the cost of discipleship, but the picture of careful royal counsel fits the Kural well.

islam.quote_or_event: “[Joseph] said, ‘You will plant for seven years consecutively; and what you harvest leave in its spikes, except a little from which you will eat.’”
islam.explanation: Joseph advises the king of Egypt on what to do (plant), when (seven years), and how (store the grain in the ear) to get through a coming famine.
islam.tie_back: Joseph’s counsel covers the same things the Kural lists: means, timing, method and a hard task.
islam._accuracy_note: Joseph acts here as a royal adviser giving a plan of means, time and method; a strong narrative match.

judaism.quote_or_event: “To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven:”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet teaches that every action has its proper time.
judaism.tie_back: Kaalam, the right time, is one of the four things the Kural’s minister must master.
judaism._accuracy_note: Matches only the timing element; Kohelet is reflecting on life in general, not on statecraft.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “And how is a monk one with a sense of time? There is the case where a monk knows the time: ‘This is the time for recitation; this, the time for questioning; this, the time for making an effort [in meditation]; this, the time for seclusion.’”
buddhism.explanation: Among seven marks of a worthy person, the Buddha lists knowing the right time for each kind of activity.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the sutta treats knowing the right time as a skill a capable person must have.
buddhism.source: Dhammaññu Sutta, Anguttara Nikaya 7.64 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Shares the emphasis on timing, but it is monastic practice, not affairs of state.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Kairos, the Greek personification of the opportune moment, was shown by the sculptor Lysippus as a youth with a lock of hair in front and a bald head behind. The point was that the right moment can be grasped as it comes but not once it has passed.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greeks made the fleeting right moment into a divine figure that had to be seized at once.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural lists kaalam, knowing the right time, as a core skill of the counsellor.
greek_mythology.source: Posidippus, epigram on the Kairos of Lysippus (Greek Anthology 16.275), summarized via Theoi Project
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Covers only the timing element; a personification rather than a teaching about ministers.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “…excellence in deliberation, which is rightness with regard to the expedient-rightness in respect both of the end, the manner, and the time.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle defines good deliberation (euboulia) as getting right what is useful, including the goal, the way it is done, and the timing.
philosophy.tie_back: End, manner and time closely match the Kural’s task, method and time.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VI.9 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: A remarkably close conceptual match; Aristotle is describing a virtue of any practically wise person, not specifically a minister.

kurals.tamil:
வன்கண் குடிகாத்தல் கற்றறிதல் ஆள்வினையோடு
ஐந்துடன் மாண்டது அமைச்சு.
kurals.transliteration:
Vankan kudikaaththal katrarithal aalvinaiyodu
Aindhudan maandadhu amaichchu.
kurals.meaning: A minister excels in firm courage, protecting the people, learning and understanding, and persevering effort, together with the five qualities already named.
kurals.elementary: A good class monitor is brave enough to speak up, looks after classmates, keeps learning, and does not give up when a job gets hard. This kural says a good adviser needs all of these together, not just one.
kurals.university: The couplet names further qualities: vankan (firmness or fearlessness, literally ‘hard eye’), kudikaaththal (protecting the subjects), katrarithal (knowing through study), and aalvinai (sustained effort, the subject of chapter 62). The phrase aindhudan (‘with the five’) is read in more than one way. In the Parimelazhagar tradition it refers back to the qualities already listed, so the minister has these as well as those. Mu. Varadarasanar splits kudi as noble birth (kudippirappu) and kaaththal as protection so that the verse itself lists five. Puliyur Kesikan instead takes the five as the purity of the five senses. Solomon Pappaiah divides katru and arithal into learning from books and learning by listening to the learned. The older-orthography edition prints ‘katrarithalaalvinaiyo / daindhudan’, which is the same text with a different word division.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “…possessed of foresight, wise, of strong memory, bold, eloquent, skilful, intelligent, possessed of enthusiasm, dignity and endurance…”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya gives a long list of qualities for a minister, including wisdom, boldness, learning and staying power.
hinduism.tie_back: Boldness, learning and endurance match the Kural’s vankan, katrarithal and aalvinai almost one for one.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close list of ministerial virtues; Kautilya’s list is much longer and does not single out protecting the people.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Wherefore, brethren, look ye out among you seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business.”
christianity.explanation: The apostles pick administrators to care for the community’s needy, requiring good character and wisdom.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it chooses officials by character and wisdom so that they can look after the people.
christianity._accuracy_note: A real parallel in appointing capable officers to serve a community, though these are church stewards, not royal ministers.

islam.quote_or_event: “One of the women said, ‘O my father, hire him. Indeed, the best one you can hire is the strong and the trustworthy.’”
islam.explanation: A daughter of Madyan urges her father to employ Moses because he is both strong and trustworthy.
islam.tie_back: Strength and reliability match the Kural’s firmness and dependable protection of those in one’s care.
islam._accuracy_note: Classical Islamic political writing often cites this verse for choosing officials, but the scene itself is about hiring a shepherd.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Moreover thou shalt provide out of all the people able men, such as fear God, men of truth, hating unjust gain; and place such over them, to be rulers of thousands, rulers of hundreds, rulers of fifties, and rulers of tens.”
judaism.explanation: Jethro advises Moses to share his burden by appointing capable, honest men to govern and judge the people.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, Jethro sets out the qualities of those who help a leader rule and protect the people.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match: Jethro, himself a counsellor, describes the qualities of officials; he stresses integrity more than courage or learning.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Kutadanta Sutta, the Buddha tells of a wise royal chaplain who advises a king to deal with banditry by giving seed to farmers, capital to traders, and proper wages to officials, rather than by punishment. The kingdom becomes prosperous and safe.
buddhism.explanation: The ideal counsellor here protects the people by fixing the economic causes of disorder.
buddhism.tie_back: This is kudikaaththal, protecting the people, carried out through wise and learned counsel.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good match for protecting the people through counsel; the story is really a critique of sacrifice, so this is a secondary theme.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Odysseus leaves for Troy he puts his old friend Mentor in charge of his household. In the Ithacan assembly, Mentor boldly rebukes the people for allowing the suitors to waste the absent king’s estate.
greek_mythology.explanation: Mentor is the trusted steward who guards what belongs to his lord and speaks out bravely.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He shows two of the Kural’s qualities, courage (vankan) and protection of those in his charge.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Fits courage and guardianship; Mentor looks after one household, not a kingdom’s people.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero reminds those who take charge of public affairs of two rules from Plato: to keep the good of the citizens so clearly in view that everything they do serves it, and to care for the whole body politic rather than one part of it.
philosophy.explanation: For Cicero, the first duty of a statesman is to protect the welfare of all citizens, not a faction.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s kudikaaththal, protecting the people, as a basic mark of a minister.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong match on protecting the people; Cicero does not list the other qualities in this passage.

kurals.tamil:
பிரித்தலும் பேணிக் கொளலும் பிரிந்தார்ப்
பொருத்தலும் வல்ல தமைச்சு.
kurals.transliteration:
Piriththalum paenik kolalum pirindhaarp
Poruththalum valla thamaichchu.
kurals.meaning: A minister is skilled at splitting the enemy’s allies away, keeping his own side loyal, and bringing back those who have broken away.
kurals.elementary: Imagine two teams in a playground game. A clever captain can persuade kids who are thinking of joining the other team to stay neutral, keep his own teammates happy, and make friends again with anyone who left in a huff. This kural says a good adviser has those three skills.
kurals.university: The couplet names three diplomatic skills. Piriththal is detaching allies from the enemy. Paenik kolal is keeping one’s own supporters, which Solomon Pappaiah explains as keeping them through gifts and kind words. Pirindhaar poruththal is reconciling those who have left. Commentators link these to the classical upayas (means of statecraft): bheda (division), dana (gifts) and sama (conciliation). Kautilya treats the same means at length. The last words, valla thamaichchu, are an older way of writing valladhu amaichchu (‘the minister is one capable of’), and all three sources agree on the text. Varadarasanar’s gloss and Kalaignar’s specify that those to be divided are the enemy’s helpers, which keeps the verse within fair statecraft rather than general intrigue.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Before the Kurukshetra war, Krishna travels to Hastinapura as envoy to try to reconcile the Kauravas and the Pandavas. He first appeals for peace and offers a settlement. He also warns Duryodhana’s allies and elders about the cost of war, which works on the loyalties within the Kaurava camp.
hinduism.explanation: Krishna’s embassy uses conciliation, offers and division, the classical upayas, in one mission.
hinduism.tie_back: It shows the Kural’s three skills of reconciling, retaining and dividing as the work of a counsellor-envoy.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (Bhagavat-yana section), trans. K. M. Ganguli
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good fit for reconciliation and division; the embassy fails, and Krishna is a divine envoy, not a minister.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And when he had so said, there arose a dissension between the Pharisees and the Sadducees: and the multitude was divided.”
christianity.explanation: On trial before the council, Paul declares himself a Pharisee on the question of resurrection, which splits his hostile judges into two factions.
christianity.tie_back: This is piriththal, dividing an opposing party, done with a single well-judged word.
christianity._accuracy_note: A clear example of dividing opponents; Paul is defending himself, not advising a ruler.

islam.quote_or_event: “And hold firmly to the rope of Allah all together and do not become divided. And remember the favor of Allah upon you - when you were enemies and He brought your hearts together and you became, by His favor, brothers.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an reminds the believers that once-hostile groups were reconciled into brotherhood and warns them against splitting apart.
islam.tie_back: It praises the Kural’s last two skills, holding one’s own people together and reuniting those who were divided.
islam._accuracy_note: Matches keeping and reuniting; the verse credits God rather than a minister and does not cover dividing enemies.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Absalom and all the men of Israel said: ‘The counsel of Hushai the Archite is better than the counsel of Ahithophel.’—For the LORD had ordained to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel, to the intent that the LORD might bring evil upon Absalom.”
judaism.explanation: David sends his loyal friend Hushai into the rebel Absalom’s council, where Hushai’s advice overturns Ahithophel’s dangerous plan.
judaism.tie_back: Hushai breaks up the enemy’s counsel from within while staying loyal to his king. This is piriththal carried out by a counsellor.
judaism._accuracy_note: An excellent narrative example of a loyal counsellor dividing the enemy camp; the text credits the outcome to God’s design.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Maha-parinibbana Sutta, King Ajatasattu sends his minister Vassakara to ask the Buddha about attacking the Vajjians. The Buddha lists seven conditions, among them meeting often and in harmony, that keep the Vajjians strong. Vassakara concludes that they cannot be conquered by force, only through diplomacy or by breaking up their unity.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta shows both sides: unity protects a people, and a shrewd minister sees that division is the way to defeat them.
buddhism.tie_back: It sets keeping one’s people together against dividing an opponent, the two poles of the Kural’s verse.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Direct match on dividing and preserving alliances, with an actual minister; the Buddha’s own concern is harmony, not conquest.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After Achilles withdraws from the fighting in anger, Agamemnon sends Odysseus, Ajax and old Phoenix to him with offers of gifts to win him back to the Greek army.
greek_mythology.explanation: The embassy is a formal attempt to reconcile an estranged ally through gifts and persuasion.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is pirindhaar poruththal, bringing back those who have split away, which the Kural counts as a minister’s skill.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Clear example of reconciliation by envoys, although in Book 9 it fails.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Sun Tzu advises that when the enemy’s forces are united they should be separated, and he treats breaking up the enemy’s alliances as better than attacking his army in the field.
philosophy.explanation: Classical Chinese strategy puts diplomatic division before open battle.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s first skill, piriththal, as a doctrine of statecraft.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War I and III (trans. Lionel Giles)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong match on dividing enemies; Sun Tzu says little about reconciling former allies.

kurals.tamil:
தெரிதலும் தேர்ந்து செயலும் ஒருதலையாச்
சொல்லலும் வல்லது அமைச்சு.
kurals.transliteration:
Theridhalum thaerndhu seyalum orudhalaiyaach
Sollalum valladhu amaichchu.
kurals.meaning: A minister can study a matter thoroughly, act only after careful choice, and state a firm, clear conclusion.
kurals.elementary: A good referee watches the play closely, thinks for a moment, and then makes a clear call. He does not say “maybe”. This kural says a good adviser looks carefully, chooses wisely, and then speaks clearly.
kurals.university: Three abilities are named. Theridhal is examining or understanding the matter. Thaerndhu seyal is acting after deliberate selection of means. Orudhalaiyaach sollal is speaking decisively (orudhalai, ‘one-sided’, i.e. unambiguous). Commentators differ on the last. Varadarasanar and Kesikan take it as boldness and clarity, while Solomon Pappaiah stresses asserting only what is beneficial. The Parimelazhagar tradition ties it to giving the king a settled opinion rather than a list of options, much as Kautilya’s teacher Pishuna asks for counsellors ‘capable of giving decisive opinion’. ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net read valladhu amaichu, and thirukkural-thamizh.org prints the older form ‘valla thamaichchu’. The two are the same words divided differently.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Hence he shall consult such persons as are believed to be capable of giving decisive opinion regarding those works about which he seeks far advice.”
hinduism.explanation: In the Arthashastra’s debate on counsel, the teacher Pishuna argues that a king should consult men who can give firm, decisive advice rather than half-hearted opinions.
hinduism.tie_back: This is orudhalaiyaach sollal, the decisive word, which the Kural requires of a minister.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Precise match on decisive counsel; Kautilya presents it as one view in a debate and then qualifies it.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that speech should be plain and definite, without evasive hedging or extra oaths.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural likewise praises the minister who can say one clear thing.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches the ideal of unambiguous speech; Jesus is talking about oaths and honesty, not political advice.

islam.quote_or_event: “So pardon them and ask forgiveness for them and consult them in the matter. And when you have decided, then rely upon Allah.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet is told to consult his companions and, once a decision is made, to carry it out with trust in God.
islam.tie_back: This follows the Kural’s order: think it through, decide, then act firmly.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match for deliberation followed by resolute action; here the ruler consults rather than a minister advising.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Every purpose is established by counsel; and with good advice carry on war.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs teaches that plans succeed when built on deliberation, and that even war must be waged by wise guidance.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s thaerndhu seyal: acting only after deliberate choice.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close match on counsel before action; it does not address speaking decisively.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Kalama Sutta, the Buddha tells the Kalamas not to accept teachings on report, tradition or a teacher’s authority alone. They should examine them, and once they know for themselves what is skilful and beneficial, adopt and practise it.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lays out a method of careful examination followed by committed action.
buddhism.tie_back: It follows the Kural’s sequence of theridhal (examining) and then thaerndhu seyal (acting on what one has chosen).
buddhism._accuracy_note: Parallel in method only; the sutta is about religious belief, not counsel to a ruler.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Trapped in the Cyclops’ cave, Odysseus first wants to stab the sleeping Polyphemus. He stops himself when he realizes that his men could never move the huge stone from the doorway. He works out a slower plan (the wine, the blinding stake and the escape under the rams) and carries it through.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus checks his impulse, thinks the situation through, and then acts on a well-chosen plan.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This shows the Kural’s ideal of examining a situation and acting only after careful choice.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good illustration of deliberation before action; Odysseus acts for himself rather than advising a king.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Discourse on Method, Descartes’ second provisional maxim is to be as firm and resolute in action as he can. Once he has settled on a course, even a doubtful one, he follows it steadily, like travellers lost in a forest who should walk straight in one direction rather than wander in circles.
philosophy.explanation: Descartes argues that after reasonable deliberation, being decisive is itself a practical virtue.
philosophy.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s thaerndhu seyal and its firm, one-directional conclusion.
philosophy.source: Descartes, Discourse on Method, Part III
philosophy._accuracy_note: Parallel on resolute action after choice; Descartes is writing about personal conduct, not statecraft.

kurals.tamil:
அறனறிந்து ஆன்றமைந்த சொல்லான்எஞ் ஞான்றுந்
திறனறிந்தான் தேர்ச்சித் துணை.
kurals.transliteration:
Aranarindhu aandramaindha sollaan enjnjaandrum
Thiranarindhaan thaerchchith thunai.
kurals.meaning: The best partner in deliberation is one who knows what is right, speaks with full learning and restraint, and always knows how things are to be done.
kurals.elementary: When you need advice about something hard, you go to the person who knows right from wrong, speaks calmly and carefully, and knows the practical steps. This kural says that kind of person is the best helper for a leader.
kurals.university: The couplet sets out three qualifications for a thaerchchith thunai, a ‘companion in deliberation’. The first is aranarindhu, knowing aram (dharma or righteousness). The second is aandramaindha sollaan, one whose speech is full (aandru, ‘abundant, filled with learning’) and measured (amaindha, ‘settled, restrained’). The third is enjnjaandrum thiranarindhaan, one who always knows the method. Commentators differ over whether aandru points to learning, as Varadarasanar and Pappaiah take it, or to maturity. Pappaiah reads amaindha as modest or restrained speech. Parimelazhagar’s reading places moral knowledge first, so the counsellor’s skill serves aram rather than mere expediency. All three editions agree on the text; the older one divides it as ‘aranarindh aandramaindha sollaanenjnjaandrun’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He whom neither anger nor joy, nor pride, nor false modesty, nor stupefaction, nor vanity, can draw away from the high ends of life, is considered as wise.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura, the Mahabharata’s model counsellor, describes the wise man as one whom no passion can pull away from life’s proper aims.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the aranarindhu counsellor, grounded in dharma, whom the Kural calls the best partner in deliberation.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva 33 (Vidura Niti), trans. K. M. Ganguli
hinduism._accuracy_note: Spoken by the epic’s ideal minister and centred on moral steadiness; it says less about speech or method.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man.”
christianity.explanation: Paul asks believers to speak graciously and thoughtfully, fitting each answer to the person addressed.
christianity.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural’s aandramaindha sol, full and measured speech.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches the ideal of measured speech only; not about counsel to a ruler.

islam.quote_or_event: “And those who have responded to their lord and established prayer and whose affair is [determined by] consultation among themselves, and from what We have provided them, they spend.”
islam.explanation: The surah named Ash-Shura (Consultation) lists mutual consultation among the defining traits of the faithful.
islam.tie_back: Shura makes the Kural’s thaerchchith thunai, the partner in deliberation, a religious ideal.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on consultation as a value; says nothing specific about the qualities of the counsellor.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Where no wise direction is, a people falleth; but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs teaches that a nation stands or falls by the quality of the guidance it receives.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s point is the same: a ruler needs capable counsellors beside him.
judaism._accuracy_note: Direct statement on the value of counsellors; it stresses their number rather than their personal qualities.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Speak only the speech that neither torments self nor does harm to others. That speech is truly well spoken.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes well-spoken speech as speech that harms no one.
buddhism.tie_back: This fits the Kural’s aandramaindha sol, restrained and weighty speech, as part of a good counsellor’s character.
buddhism.source: Subhasita Sutta, Sutta Nipata 3.3 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Covers the speech element only; says nothing of dharma-knowledge or practical method.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Agamemnon and Achilles quarrel, old Nestor of Pylos rises to calm them. Homer calls him the clear-voiced speaker from whose tongue words flowed sweeter than honey, and he draws on his long experience of great men.
greek_mythology.explanation: Nestor is Homer’s model counsellor: experienced, eloquent and respected by both sides.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He combines the Kural’s learned, measured speech with long practical knowledge.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong match for the eloquent, experienced counsellor, though his advice goes unheeded in this scene.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle says that a speaker earns trust through three qualities: practical wisdom (phronesis), virtue (arete) and goodwill (eunoia). A speaker who lacks any one of them gives bad or untrustworthy advice.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, credible counsel needs good judgement, good character and genuine care for the listener.
philosophy.tie_back: Virtue, wisdom and trustworthy speech correspond closely to the Kural’s aram, learned speech and practical skill.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close three-part parallel; Aristotle is analysing persuasion rather than the office of minister.

kurals.tamil:
மதிநுட்பம் நூலோடு உடையார்க்கு அதிநுட்பம்
யாவுள முன்நிற் பவை.
kurals.transliteration:
Madhinutpam noolodu udaiyaarkku adhinutpam
Yaavula munnir pavai.
kurals.meaning: What scheme, however subtle, can stand against someone who has natural sharpness of mind together with book learning?
kurals.elementary: Some kids are naturally quick at puzzles, and some have read lots of puzzle books. A kid who is both quick and well-read is very hard to trick. This kural says a good adviser is like that, so no clever trap can fool him.
kurals.university: The couplet contrasts madhinutpam, native acuteness of intellect, with nool, learning from texts, and says that someone who has both cannot be outwitted by any adhinutpam, any ‘extreme subtlety’ or stratagem. The rhetorical question yaavula munnirpavai (‘what are there that stand before [him]?’) implies ‘none’. Commentators from Parimelazhagar on distinguish iyarkai arivu (natural intelligence) from seyarkai arivu (acquired or learned intelligence). This pair prepares for kural 637, which uses the same iyarkai and seyarkai vocabulary. Kalaignar and Pappaiah read adhinutpam specifically as hostile schemes (soozhchi). There are small spelling differences, such as முன்நிற் (ytamizh.com, thirukkural.net) against முன்னிற் and the joined ‘மதிநுட்ப நூலோ டுடையார்க்’ in the older-orthography thirukkural-thamizh.org, but the wording is the same.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Duryodhana plots to burn the Pandavas in a house of lac at Varanavata, Vidura sees through the scheme. He warns Yudhishthira in veiled language that only Yudhishthira understands and secretly sends a miner to dig an escape tunnel, so the plot fails.
hinduism.explanation: Vidura’s sharpness and learning defeat an elaborate, carefully hidden conspiracy.
hinduism.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural’s claim that no stratagem can stand against natural wit joined to learning.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Jatugriha section), trans. K. M. Ganguli
hinduism._accuracy_note: An excellent narrative match with the epic’s model minister; summarized rather than quoted.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his disciples to combine shrewdness with innocence when facing hostile schemers.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it values a sharpness of mind that cannot be outwitted by others.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches the call for shrewdness; it adds moral innocence and says nothing about learning.

islam.quote_or_event: “A believer is not stung twice (by something) out of one and the same hole.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that a believer should be alert and learn from experience so as not to be deceived again the same way.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s minister is similarly too sharp to be caught by any scheme.
islam._accuracy_note: Matches the idea of not being outwitted; it stresses learning from experience rather than books.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Now as for these four youths, God gave them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom; and Daniel had understanding in all visions and dreams.”
judaism.explanation: Daniel and his companions, trained for royal service in Babylon, have both learning and a special gift of insight.
judaism.tie_back: Learning plus an inborn gift is the Kural’s nool plus madhinutpam.
judaism._accuracy_note: A close match: courtiers who combine learning and special insight (v. 20 says they were ten times better than the court magicians); the insight is presented as a divine gift.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Maha-ummagga Jataka, the Bodhisatta is born as Mahosadha, a wise minister to King Vedeha. Again and again he sees through the plots of rival ministers and of the enemy king’s counsellor Kevatta, and turns their stratagems back on them.
buddhism.explanation: Mahosadha is the Buddhist model of a minister whose wisdom no intrigue can defeat.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s claim that no subtle scheme can stand before an intelligent, well-taught minister.
buddhism._accuracy_note: An excellent match: a minister who defeats every stratagem through wisdom.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: To avoid going to Troy, Odysseus pretends to be mad and ploughs his field while sowing salt. Palamedes sees through the trick and places Odysseus’s infant son Telemachus in the plough’s path. When Odysseus swerves, the pretence is exposed.
greek_mythology.explanation: One clever man’s scheme is undone by another man’s sharper insight.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This shows the Kural’s point that a sufficiently sharp mind defeats even a subtle stratagem.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good example of wit defeating a trick; Palamedes is not a king’s minister, and learning plays no part.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Horace asks whether a good poem comes from nature or from art. He answers that he cannot see what study can do without natural talent, or what raw talent can do untrained: each needs the other’s help.
philosophy.explanation: Horace insists that native gift and disciplined learning must work together.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s pairing of madhinutpam (native acuteness) with nool (learning).
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close on nature plus learning; Horace is writing about poetry, not statecraft or outwitting schemes.

kurals.tamil:
செயற்கை அறிந்தக் கடைத்தும் உலகத்து
இயற்கை அறிந்து செயல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Seyarkai arindhak kadaiththum ulakaththu
Iyarkai arindhu seyal.
kurals.meaning: Even when you know from books how a thing should be done, act only after understanding how the world actually works.
kurals.elementary: You can read a book about riding a bicycle, but you also need to notice the real road, the bumps and the traffic. This kural says that even after learning the rules, you must look at the real world and act in a way that fits it.
kurals.university: The couplet sets seyarkai, the ‘made’ or acquired knowledge of methods found in treatises, against ulakaththu iyarkai, the natural ways of the world. The minister should act (seyal) only after knowing the second as well as the first. Mu. Varadarasanar’s gloss makes seyarkai explicitly nool arivu (book knowledge). Solomon Pappaiah extends it to methods learned from foreign books and applies iyarkai to the character of one’s own land and people. Commentators in Parimelazhagar’s tradition often recall the grammarians’ rule that ulakam, ‘world’, can mean the worthy or experienced people whose conduct sets the norm. There is a small textual variant. ytamizh.com and thirukkural-thamizh.org read arindhak kadaiththum (with the doubled k), while thirukkural.net prints arindha kadaiththum. The meaning does not change.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Even a man of knowledge acts according to his own nature, for everyone follows the nature he has acquired from the three modes. What can repression accomplish?”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna observes that even the learned must reckon with the nature of beings, which cannot simply be overridden.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it warns that knowledge must take account of how things actually are (iyarkai).
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.33 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Shares the idea that nature constrains action; the Gita’s concern is spiritual discipline, not administration.

christianity.quote_or_event: “To the weak became I as weak, that I might gain the weak: I am made all things to all men, that I might by all means save some.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes adapting his approach to the character and situation of each audience.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s advice to fit one’s method to the ways of the people one is dealing with.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good match on adapting to people as they actually are; Paul’s goal is evangelism, not statecraft.

islam.quote_or_event: “And We did not send any messenger except [speaking] in the language of his people to state clearly for them, and Allah sends astray [thereby] whom He wills and guides whom He wills.”
islam.explanation: God sends each messenger in his own people’s language so that the message fits those who hear it.
islam.tie_back: Even revealed truth is delivered in a form suited to the world it enters, as the Kural advises.
islam._accuracy_note: An analogy of adapting to the audience; the verse is about prophecy, not administration.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A person should never deviate from the local custom, as Moses ascended to heaven on high and did not eat bread while he was there, whereas the ministering angels descended down to this world, as guests visiting Abraham, and they ate bread.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Tanhum bar Hanilai teaches that one should follow the customs of the place one is in, as even Moses and the angels did.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s rule to act in keeping with ulakaththu iyarkai, the ways of the world around you.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 86b (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz)
judaism._accuracy_note: A close proverbial match on conforming to local ways; it is about custom and etiquette, not policy.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Aranavibhanga Sutta, the Buddha says that one should not insist on one’s own dialect or override ordinary usage. The same bowl is called by different names in different regions, and a wise person uses whatever word is current there instead of insisting on his own.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha warns against rigidly imposing one standard where local usage differs.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s point that correct theory must bend to the real ways of the world.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good parallel on adapting to local practice; limited to language and part of a teaching on avoiding conflict.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Shipwrecked on the Phaeacian shore, Odysseus meets the princess Nausicaa. He decides not to clasp her knees as a formal suppliant might, in case it offends her, and speaks gently from a distance instead.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus knows the formal rules of supplication but adjusts them to the real situation in front of him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s advice: know the rules, then act according to how the world actually is.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: A neat illustration of rule adjusted to circumstance; it concerns personal tact, not governance.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Nor is practical wisdom concerned with universals only-it must also recognize the particulars; for it is practical, and practice is concerned with particulars. This is why some who do not know, and especially those who have experience, are more practical than others who know…”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that general knowledge is not enough for action; one must also grasp particular circumstances, which experience provides.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s contrast between book methods (seyarkai) and knowing the world (iyarkai).
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VI.7 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: A very close conceptual match between theoretical knowledge and experienced grasp of particulars.

kurals.tamil:
அறிகொன்று அறியான் எனினும் உறுதி
உழையிருந்தான் கூறல் கடன்.
kurals.transliteration:
Arikondru ariyaan eninum urudhi
Uzhaiyirundhaan kooral kadan.
kurals.meaning: Even if the king rejects wise advice and is ignorant himself, the one who stands beside him still has a duty to tell him what is truly good.
kurals.elementary: Imagine your friend is about to do something unsafe and will not listen. A true friend still tells them the truth, even if they get grumpy. This kural says a leader’s adviser must always tell the leader what is good, even when the leader does not want to hear it.
kurals.university: Arikondru (‘having killed knowledge’) is usually taken to mean that the king destroys or ignores the counsel of those who know. Ariyaan eninum (‘even if he himself does not know’) adds that he also lacks knowledge of his own. Even then urudhi (what is truly and lastingly beneficial) must be told (kooral kadan, ‘speaking is a duty’) by the uzhaiyirundhaan, ‘the one who is at his side’, meaning the minister. Solomon Pappaiah stresses that the minister must speak without anger and without fear. Kalaignar applies the verse to those near any ruler. The couplet is the moral centre of the chapter: the minister’s duty to give frank counsel does not depend on whether it will be welcomed. The thirukkural-thamizh.org edition prints ‘arikon rariyaa neninu murudhi / yuzhaiyirundhaan’, a difference of word division only.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “They are abundant, O king, that can always speak agreeable words. The speaker, however, is rare, as also the hearer, of words that are disagreeable but medicinal.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura tells the blind king Dhritarashtra, whose sons are heading for ruin, that honest but unwelcome advice is rare.
hinduism.tie_back: Vidura is doing what the Kural requires: telling a king who will not listen what is good for him.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva 37 (Vidura Niti), trans. K. M. Ganguli
hinduism._accuracy_note: A near-exact situational and moral match: the model minister counselling an unheeding king.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For John had said unto Herod, It is not lawful for thee to have thy brother’s wife.”
christianity.explanation: John the Baptist confronts King Herod about his unlawful marriage, and it later costs him his life.
christianity.tie_back: He shows the Kural’s duty to tell a ruler the truth whatever the cost.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong on fearless truth-telling to a ruler; John is a prophet, not a court adviser.

islam.quote_or_event: “The Religion is sincerity.” We said, “To whom?” He said “To Allah, to His Book, To His Messenger, and to the leaders of the Muslims and their masses.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet defines religion as nasiha, sincere good counsel, owed even to those in authority.
islam.tie_back: This makes the Kural’s duty to give leaders sincere advice part of faith itself.
islam._accuracy_note: Close match on the duty of sincere counsel to rulers; it does not address a ruler who refuses it.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Nathan said to David: ‘Thou art the man.’”
judaism.explanation: After telling David a parable about a rich man who stole a poor man’s lamb, the prophet Nathan confronts the king directly over his sin with Bathsheba and Uriah.
judaism.tie_back: Nathan, a member of David’s court, tells his king the unwelcome truth, as the Kural requires of the one at the ruler’s side.
judaism._accuracy_note: Classic example of a court figure speaking hard truth to a king; unlike the Kural’s king, David repents.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In the case of words that the Tathagata knows to be factual, true, beneficial, but unendearing & disagreeable to others, he has a sense of the proper time for saying them.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells Prince Abhaya that he will speak true and beneficial words even when they are unwelcome, choosing the right moment.
buddhism.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s urudhi, beneficial counsel given even when it will be disliked.
buddhism.source: Abhaya Sutta, Majjhima Nikaya 58 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong match on voicing unwelcome but beneficial truths; the Buddha is teaching a prince, not serving a king.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Before the fighting at the Greek ships, the Trojan counsellor Polydamas urges Hector to withdraw the army inside the city walls now that Achilles has returned. Hector angrily rejects the advice, and the Trojans suffer heavy losses. Hector later admits that he should have listened.
greek_mythology.explanation: Polydamas gives honest counsel to a leader who will not listen.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s situation: a counsellor at the leader’s side whose sound advice is spurned.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Very close narrative match: a counsellor speaks, is rebuffed, and is proved right.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plutarch argues that the true friend is known by his frank speech (parrhesia). He is willing to point out a man’s faults for his good, while the flatterer only says what pleases. Plutarch adds that this frankness should be used with tact and at the right moment.
philosophy.explanation: For Plutarch, honest criticism given for the other person’s benefit is the sign of real loyalty.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the minister’s duty in the Kural to speak urudhi, what is truly beneficial.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, How to Tell a Flatterer from a Friend (Moralia)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close in spirit; Plutarch discusses friendship generally, though he repeatedly applies it to rulers and their courtiers.

kurals.tamil:
பழுதெண்ணும் மந்திரியின் பக்கததுள் தெவ்வோர்
எழுபது கோடி உறும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Pazhudhennum mandhiriyin pakkadhadhul thevvor
Ezhubadhu kodi urum.
kurals.meaning: Seventy crores of open enemies are better than one minister at your side who plots your ruin.
kurals.elementary: A lot of rivals on the other team are easier to handle than one teammate who is secretly trying to make you lose. This kural says a bad adviser close to a leader is more dangerous than a huge army of enemies.
kurals.university: Pazhudhennum mandhiri is ‘the minister who contemplates harm’. Mandhiri is from the Sanskrit mantrin; it stands beside the chapter’s Tamil amaichu. Pakkaththul means ‘at one’s side, within one’s own ranks’. Thevvor ezhubadhu kodi (seventy crores of enemies) is hyperbole for a countless host. There is a real textual and grammatical point here. ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net read mandhiriyin, while the older-orthography thirukkural-thamizh.org reads mandhiriyir (‘mandhiriyir pakkadhadhut tevvo’). Both are forms of the ablative of comparison, ‘than the minister’. That is why Varadarasanar, Kalaignar and Kesikan read ‘seventy crore foes are better than such a minister’. Solomon Pappaiah reads it instead as ‘such a minister equals seventy crore foes’ and glosses pazhudhu as self-interest over the nation’s good.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Shakuni, Duryodhana’s maternal uncle and closest adviser, devises the rigged game of dice through which the Pandavas lose their kingdom. His counsel drives the Kauravas step by step toward the war that destroys them.
hinduism.explanation: Shakuni is the epic’s archetype of the evil counsellor at a prince’s side.
hinduism.tie_back: He shows the Kural’s warning that one adviser who thinks harm can ruin more surely than a host of enemies.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva (Dyuta section), trans. K. M. Ganguli
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative match; Shakuni works against the Pandavas rather than against his own master, although his advice ultimately destroys the Kauravas too.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I speak not of you all: I know whom I have chosen: but that the scripture may be fulfilled, He that eateth bread with me hath lifted up his heel against me.”
christianity.explanation: At the Last Supper, Jesus foretells betrayal by one of his own inner circle, Judas.
christianity.tie_back: The deepest harm comes from one at one’s side, as the Kural warns.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong on betrayal from within the inner circle; Judas is a disciple, not a counsellor.

islam.quote_or_event: “Allah never sends a prophet or gives the Caliphate to a Caliph but that he (the prophet or the Caliph) has two groups of advisors: A group advising him to do good and exhorts him to do it, and the other group advising him to do evil and exhorts him to do it.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet warns that every ruler has an inner circle, and part of it will push him toward evil.
islam.tie_back: This names the Kural’s danger, the harmful adviser at the ruler’s side, as a permanent feature of power.
islam._accuracy_note: A direct match on evil counsellors in a ruler’s inner circle.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For it was not an enemy that taunted me, then I could have borne it; neither was it mine adversary that did magnify himself against me, then I would have hid myself from him. But it was thou, a man mine equal, my companion, and my familiar friend; We took sweet counsel together…”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist says an enemy’s attack could be endured, but betrayal by a trusted companion and fellow counsellor cannot. Tradition often links this to Ahithophel, David’s adviser who joined Absalom’s revolt.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s claim that the enemy within is worse than any number of foes outside.
judaism._accuracy_note: A close emotional and structural parallel; the link to Ahithophel comes from tradition, not the text.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Devadatta befriends Prince Ajatasattu and urges him to kill his father, King Bimbisara, and take the throne while Devadatta takes over the Sangha. The prince follows this counsel, and the kingdom and the Sangha both suffer for it.
buddhism.explanation: Devadatta is the Buddhist figure of the corrupt counsellor whose advice leads a prince to ruin.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s pazhudhennum mandhiri, the adviser at one’s side who plots harm.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good match on a harmful intimate adviser; Devadatta is a monk, not a minister.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When the Greeks pretend to sail away from Troy, they leave Sinon behind. He convinces the Trojans to bring the wooden horse inside their walls, and at night he signals the Greek fleet to return, so the city that had withstood ten years of siege falls from within.
greek_mythology.explanation: One deceiver inside the walls achieved what the whole Greek army could not.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This makes vivid the Kural’s claim that one enemy at your side is worse than a vast host outside.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong on the danger of the enemy within; Sinon is an infiltrator, not a trusted minister.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Machiavelli writes that a prince can judge a minister simply: when the minister thinks more of his own interests than the prince’s and seeks his own profit in everything, he will never be a good minister and can never be trusted.
philosophy.explanation: For Machiavelli, the self-serving minister is a fundamental danger to the state.
philosophy.tie_back: This follows Solomon Pappaiah’s reading of the Kural’s pazhudhu as self-interest over the nation’s good.
philosophy.source: Machiavelli, The Prince, ch. 22 (trans. W. K. Marriott)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close on the self-serving minister; it lacks the Kural’s comparison with external enemies.

kurals.tamil:
முறைப்படச் சூழ்ந்தும் முடிவிலவே செய்வர்
திறப்பாடு இலாஅ தவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Muraippadach soozhndhum mudivilavae seyvar
Thirappaadu ilaaa thavar.
kurals.meaning: Those without the skill to carry things through will leave their work unfinished, even when they have planned it properly.
kurals.elementary: You can draw a perfect plan for a sandcastle, but if you do not know how to pack the sand, it falls apart halfway. This kural says a good plan is not enough; an adviser also needs the skill to finish the job.
kurals.university: Muraippadach soozhndhum means ‘even having deliberated in due order’, where soozhchi is the technical term for counsel. Such people mudivilavae seyvar, ‘do only things without completion’, if they are thirappaadu ilaadhavar, lacking executive ability. Ilaaa carries a prosodic lengthening (alapedai) needed for the metre. The thirukkural-thamizh.org edition prints ‘thirappaa delaaa thavar’, the older joined spelling of thirappaadu + ilaaa. Varadarasanar and Pappaiah take mudivila to mean half-done or defective work, while Kesikan reads it as ‘endless’, never-concluding activity. Closing the chapter this way balances its stress on deliberation. Counsel without execution fails, which leads into the later chapters on action (vinaiththooimai, vinaiththitpam, vinaiseyalvagai, 66-68).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A man engaged in devotional service rids himself of both good and bad reactions even in this life. Therefore strive for yoga, which is the art of all work.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna’s phrase yogah karmasu kaushalam, often rendered ‘yoga is skill in action’, makes skilful execution itself a spiritual ideal.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural likewise says that without skill in action (thirappaadu) even good planning fails.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.50 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Shares the value of skill in action; the Gita’s context is freedom from karmic reaction, not administrative competence.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it? Lest haply, after he hath laid the foundation, and is not able to finish it, all that behold it begin to mock him, Saying, This man began to build, and was not able to finish.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus pictures a builder who lays foundations but cannot complete the tower and becomes a laughing stock.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s mudivila: work begun but never finished.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong image of unfinished work; Jesus blames poor planning, whereas the Kural blames poor execution after good planning.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do? Great is hatred in the sight of Allah that you say what you do not do.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an condemns people whose words and plans are not carried into action.
islam.tie_back: This parallels the Kural’s rebuke of those who plan well but cannot complete the deed.
islam._accuracy_note: Parallel on the gap between words and deeds; the Qur’an treats it as a moral failure, the Kural as a lack of competence.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Study is not the most important thing, but actions; whoever indulges in too many words brings about sin.”
judaism.explanation: Shimon ben Gamliel teaches that what counts is doing, not merely learning or talking.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ranks carrying things out above deliberation alone.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good match on action over study; it concerns religious practice rather than executive skill.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Like a beautiful flower full of colour but without fragrance, even so, fruitless are the fair words of one who does not practise them.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada compares good words that are not practised to a flower that looks fine but has no scent.
buddhism.tie_back: In the same way, well-made plans that are never carried out, as the Kural warns, bear no fruit.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close image of fine words without results; the verse concerns practising the Dhamma, not carrying out policy.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Plato’s myth, Epimetheus asks to hand out the gods’ gifts to the animals himself. He shares out speed, strength, fur and claws with careful balance, but uses them all up before he reaches human beings, who are left naked and defenceless until Prometheus steals fire for them.
greek_mythology.explanation: Epimetheus (‘afterthought’) carries out a well-intended plan without the skill to finish it properly.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He shows the Kural’s person who plans properly but leaves the work incomplete.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good mythic picture of incomplete execution; Epimetheus fails through lack of foresight as much as lack of skill.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle argues that virtue has to be active, not just possessed: just as at the Olympic Games it is not the finest and strongest who are crowned but those who compete, so in life it is those who act rightly who win the prize.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, capacity or intention without effective action achieves nothing.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural similarly says that right deliberation without skill in execution is worthless.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics I.8 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Parallel on action over mere potential; Aristotle’s subject is happiness, not administrative execution.
